## Chapter 1. Introduction to Causality

[Go to chapter](/notes/01-introduction.html)

::: {.recall}
The observed outcome is a **collapse** of the potential-outcome pair. The other
half — the {{< term counterfactual >}} — is not merely unknown, it is
unobservable in principle. This is the [fundamental problem of causal
inference](/glossary.qmd#term-fundamental-problem) [@holland1986].

[Context](/notes/01-introduction.html#recall-1)
:::

::: {.recall}
In the potential-outcomes table a **causal** contrast is read *down a column* —
the same people under two regimes. The naive contrast is read *across the two
observed cells* — different people under different regimes. Every method in
this course is a way of filling in one counterfactual cell so that a column
can be read.

[Context](/notes/01-introduction.html#recall-2)
:::

::: {.recall}
Naive difference = ATT + {{< term selection-bias >}}. Selection bias is not
noise and not sampling error: it does not shrink as the sample grows. More
data makes a wrong answer more precise, not more correct.

[Context](/notes/01-introduction.html#recall-3)
:::

::: {.quiz question="The sample grows from 4,000 to 400,000 observations. What happens to the bias in the second design?"}
Nothing. Selection bias is a property of the **assignment mechanism**, not of
the sample size. Only precision improves: the confidence interval tightens
around the very same wrong number.

This is what separates bias from random error, and it is why "we have millions
of rows" is not an argument in a causal question.
:::

::: {.quiz question="Why not simply put every available variable into the regression?"}
Because variables come in kinds that must be handled differently.
Controlling for a {{< term confounder >}} removes bias; controlling for a
collider creates it. The data cannot tell them apart — only an assumed causal
structure can.

The consequence: choosing controls is a decision made **before** looking at
the data, on the basis of subject-matter knowledge.
:::

::: {.recall}
Methods of causal inference differ less in their mathematics than in **which
untestable assumption** they demand in exchange for randomization. Judge a
method by how plausible its assumption is in the problem at hand, not by how
sophisticated its machinery looks.

[Context](/notes/01-introduction.html#recall-4)
:::


## Bias from Confounding

[Go to chapter](/explorables/confounding-bias.html)

::: {.recall}
A single estimate misses the truth by **bias plus noise**, and only noise
shrinks with the sample size. An estimate stabilising as data accumulates is
therefore no evidence that it is stabilising on the truth: a biased estimator
converges too — neatly, confidently, and onto the wrong number.

[Context](/explorables/confounding-bias.html#recall-1)
:::

::: {.recall}
Bias from confounding is a property of the assignment mechanism. It survives
any sample size, and it does not depend on how large the true effect is. Only
a change in the design — or an assumption that substitutes for one — removes
it.

[Context](/explorables/confounding-bias.html#recall-2)
:::

::: {.quiz question="With the confounder at zero the bias readout stays at 0.00, yet a single estimate still misses the true ATE — and misses by less as n grows. Is that bias?"}
No, it is noise. At strength 0 assignment is a fair coin that knows nothing
about the potential outcomes, so $\mathbb{E}[\hat\tau] = \tau$ exactly: the
estimator is unbiased, and the dashed truth line runs through the middle of the
cloud at *every* sample size.

What shrinks is the width of that cloud, at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$. Bias is a
statement about where the cloud is centred; the sample size only controls how
tightly it is packed.

The trap is that a real study gives you one dot and no truth line, so from
inside it the two are indistinguishable. Telling them apart is always a claim
about the design, never a reading off the data.
:::

::: {.quiz question="The bias curve starts flat, bends sharply upward, then straightens out. Does it level off if you push the confounder far enough?"}
No — it keeps climbing, and asymptotically in a straight line. Worth being
precise about, because the curve *looks* like it is heading for a plateau.

One slider is driving two channels at once. It sets how strongly $x$ selects
who gets treated, and it also sets how strongly $x$ moves the outcome, since
$y_0 = 10 + c\,x + \varepsilon$. The selection channel genuinely does saturate:
past a certain strength nearly every high-$x$ unit is already treated and
nearly every low-$x$ unit already is not, so the gap
$\mathbb{E}[x \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[x \mid T=0]$ tops out at
$4\varphi(0) \approx 1.60$. The outcome channel never saturates, so the product

$$\text{bias} = c \cdot \big(\mathbb{E}[x \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[x \mid T=0]\big)$$

grows without bound — quadratically near zero, then linearly with slope
$\approx 1.60$.

The lesson is about the model rather than the world: when one knob drives two
mechanisms, the shape of the resulting curve belongs to neither of them.
:::

## Anki export

The cards are written to a TSV file on every site build:

[Download anki-cards.tsv](anki-cards.tsv){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

Import with **File → Import**, note type `Basic`, separator `Tab`, map the
third field to `Tags`, and enable **Allow HTML in fields**. Formulas arrive in
`\(...\)` and `\[...\]` notation, which Anki renders through MathJax with no
extra setup.
